title: Florida Can Enforce Ban on Social Media Accounts for Children Under 14
excerpt: An appeals court panel vacated the injunction blocking HB 3, finding the law targets addictive platform features rather than speech — and clearing Florida to act against accounts held by younger children.
body:
• A unanimous three-judge panel of the 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Wednesday that Florida can enforce HB 3, which bars children under 14 from holding accounts on platforms with addictive features.
  • Children aged 14 and 15 can use covered platforms only with parental consent; platforms face fines of up to $50,000 per violation.
  • The court held the law regulates platform features, not speech content, so it likely survives the First Amendment challenge brought by NetChoice and the CCIA.
  • For parents in the diaspora: if your child is under 14 and on Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat in Florida, those accounts are now exposed to enforcement — review them and expect age-verification prompts.

Florida can enforce its law barring children under 14 from social media, a federal appeals court ruled on Wednesday, handing the state a major win in its fight with the tech industry over how platforms treat young users. The unanimous three-judge panel of the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court's preliminary injunction that had blocked the law, known as HB 3, according to Reuters.

What the Law Requires

HB 3, signed by Governor Ron DeSantis in 2024 and among the most restrictive state laws of its kind, bars social media platforms that use so-called addictive features — infinite scroll, push notifications, autoplay video, livestreaming and visible reaction counts — from allowing children under 14 to create accounts. Teenagers aged 14 and 15 may hold accounts only with parental consent. Platforms that knowingly violate the ban can be fined up to $50,000 per violation.

https://x.com/nypost/status/2110531241887895878

Tech industry groups NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, whose members include Meta Platforms, TikTok and Snap, sued in 2024 to block the law. A federal judge in 2025 concluded the law was likely unconstitutional and issued an injunction; the appeals court's decision reverses that order and returns the case to federal court in Tallahassee for further proceedings.

Why the Court Sided With Florida

Writing for the panel, Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom held that HB 3 applies to platforms without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas conveyed on them — in his words, Truth Social is just as likely to be affected as Instagram. Because the law targets features and account access rather than content, the panel applied intermediate scrutiny rather than the strictest constitutional test, and found that Florida has an important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction and related harms. The law, the court noted, is limited by age, covers only certain platforms and features, and restricts account creation rather than access to the platforms altogether.

"HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them."

— Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals

The industry groups signalled the fight is not over. Paul Taske of the NetChoice Litigation Center said the group is evaluating all options as it continues the fight to protect Floridians' free expression and keep parents in the driver's seat. Matt Schruers, president of the CCIA, called the ruling deeply concerning, warning that it risks imposing identity authentication on internet users of all ages.

What It Means for Families

For Indian American families in Florida — one of the largest diaspora communities in the state, concentrated around Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville and South Florida — the practical effect is immediate. Platforms covered by the law can now be pressed to terminate or block accounts held by children under 14, and parents of 14- and 15-year-olds should expect consent and age-verification flows. Parents who want their younger children to stay connected with family in India will need to rely on their own accounts or on messaging services outside the law's feature-based definition.

What Happens Next

The ruling lifts the injunction; it does not end the lawsuit. The case returns to the district court, and the industry groups can seek further review. Other states are watching: Virginia, Mississippi, California, Minnesota and New York have all moved on minors' social media use, and Florida's win gives those efforts a stronger legal footing.
